items.title: Why Old Dogs Might Be Able to Teach Alzheimer’s Researchers New Tricks
items.description:
Most people  know someone with Alzheimer’s disease . When I was growing up, my grandmother struggled with dementia, and I saw firsthand how difficult that was for our family. 
 That experience was one reason I became a  neurotoxicologist who studies  how  misshapen proteins   and inflammation  in the brain can increase over time and cause dementia. While there are ways to treat the symptoms of dementia, researchers are still in search of a cure.

items.title: Scared of Shots? A Favorite Tune Helps Mute the Pain
items.description:
Many people really hate needles. When they have to give blood or get an IV for even a small medical procedure, they may panic, tensing up their muscles and spiking their heart rate, which can amplify the pain of the poke. Some people even suffer a sustained shock of pain and anxiety after the needle has come and gone. 
 Trypanophobia , as this unfortunate condition is known, is not a rare phenomenon. A 2021  study  in  Psychological Medicine  reported that it may afflict up to one in four adults

items.title: The Placenta Is More Powerful—and More Mysterious—Than You Think
items.description: People say it looks like broccoli, a tree, a bowl, a pizza, a crescent moon, a Frisbee, a pancake. Etymologically, “pancake” is closest: Placenta means cake in Latin and comes from the Greek word plakoenta, which means flat cake. Per a Greco-Roman recipe that’s been dated to 160 B.C., in order to make the round, flat dessert called “placenta,” you need thin sheets of dough, cheese, honey, and bay leaves. items.title: See the Artemis II Crew’s Handwritten Notes Documenting the Lunar Surface
items.description: People like to say we have more computing power in our pockets than NASA used to get to the moon, but even that understates things. The Apollo guidance computer had a measly four kilobytes of RAM, while the iPhone 17 Pro Max has 12 gigabytes—an increase of roughly three million-fold. Of course the Artemis II astronauts who visited the moon earlier this year had state-of-the-art technology, not just housed in the vehicle, but in their pockets as well.
